claims.text: The parent CoCrFeMnNi alloy is equiatomic.
The FeNiCrMn alloy is derived from CoCrFeMnNi by removing Co.
The Co-free FeNiCrMn alloy has a single-phase solid-solution structure in its solidified state.
Removing Co from equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi increases the effective stacking-fault energy.
The higher stacking-fault energy reduces the nucleation and density of deformation twins.
Suppression of deformation twinning shifts plastic deformation predominantly toward dislocation slip.
The switch from twinning toward slip changes the yield and post-yield response as functions of temperature and strain rate.
Homogenization produces a single-phase homogeneous microstructure such that only dynamic dislocation-versus-twinning effects vary during testing.
Equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi is a single-phase FCC alloy with a favorable strength–ductility combination over varied temperatures.
Deformation twinning in equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi significantly contributes to its simultaneous strength and ductility.
Relative to CoCrFeMnNi, Co-free FeNiCrMn will exhibit lower deformation-twin density.
Relative to CoCrFeMnNi, Co-free FeNiCrMn will deform by a more uniform, dislocation-slip-dominated mechanism.
At intermediate temperatures and high strain rates, the Co-free alloy will have a lower or delayed strain-hardening rate relative to CoCrFeMnNi.
Differences between the alloys may be less pronounced at lower strain rates or lower temperatures where thermally activated processes prevail.
The hypothesis applies to single-phase FCC alloys from approximately room temperature to a few hundred degrees Celsius and from about 10^-3 to 10^3 s^-1.
Local chemical ordering or solute-atmosphere effects could also influence the dynamic response.

Failure to observe a statistically significant reduction in twinning together with a distinct temperature- and strain-rate-dependent mechanical response in the Co-free alloy would falsify the proposed mechanism.

contradictions.description: The material is described as being in an as-solidified solid-solution state, while the test conditions require a standard homogenization heat treatment. A homogenized state is not strictly the same processing state as an as-solidified state.
